extracted.intended_audience: scientists, jurists, logicians, and others engaged in assessing human testimony and evidence
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and evidentiary criteria for assessing the credibility, reliability, and scientific study of human testimony, with emphasis on the role of experts and on physiological/pathological limits of the brain, memory, and senses. Intended to guide scholars, legal practitioners, and scientists in reconstructing principles of evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty of witnesses (Greenleaf)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘the credit due to the testimony of witnesses depends upon, firstly, their honesty’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greenleaf places honesty as the first factor in assessing testimony. The article notes this conventional ordering but criticizes treatment that ignores other distinctions (e.g., expert vs non-expert).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability of witnesses (Greenleaf)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author highlights that conventional statements of 'ability' fail to distinguish general from special ability — i.e., non-expert versus expert — and argues that this distinction is crucial when evaluating testimony, especially for complex scientific or physiological phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number and consistency of witnesses (Greenleaf)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘thirdly, their number and the consistency of their testimony’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantity of witnesses and internal consistency are treated as a combined criterion. The author implies these are useful but insufficient when underlying sensory or cognitive limits may produce consistent yet false reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conformity with experience
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘fourthly, the conformity of their testimony with experience’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agreement with established experience or empirical knowledge is a factor in crediting testimony; however, the article warns that appeal to 'experience' can be misleading if the physiology/pathology of testimony is not considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coincidence with collateral circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘fifthly, the coincidence of their testimony with collateral circumstances’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correlation with independent facts or circumstances supports credibility. The author treats this as one of Greenleaf's classical criteria but situates it among other necessary physiological considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extraordinary claims require expert investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims such as alleged feats of levitation 'could be and should be only studied by experts' and 'experiments with living human beings could only be conducted by experts in cerebro-physiology'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For phenomena beyond ordinary sensory inspection or that implicate specialized bodily processes, rely on specially trained investigators; ordinary honest observers lack the necessary basis to settle such claims reliably.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for a definition and tests of expertness
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘one may look in vain through all the authors on logic for a satisfactory definition of an expert, or for any detailed arrangement of tests by which expertness is to be estimated.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When valuing 'ability' or expert testimony, employ explicit definitions and tests of expertise rather than assuming expertness. The article criticizes the lack of formal criteria for evaluating who qualifies as an expert.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate testimony in light of cerebro-physiology and pathology
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Human testimony comes from the human brain: the scientific study of human testimony is only possible through a knowledge of the human brain in health and disease, and is therefore a department of cerebro-physiology and pathology.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret and assess testimony with reference to brain function, disease states, and physiological limits; medical/physiological knowledge is necessary to determine when testimony is likely reliable or compromised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize limitations of the human brain in health
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The Limitations of the Human Brain in Health.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The brain has very limited capacity; these inherent limits (e.g., on attention, processing speed, number of distinct thoughts in a given time) constrain the reliability and completeness of testimony and must be factored into evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited number and rapidity of distinct thoughts
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The number of distinct thoughts of which the mind is capable in a given time is very limited, and can be estimated by experiment…’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiments show a bounded rate of distinct ideas per minute; this limits what witnesses can attend to and accurately report during brief or complex events. Use such constraints when judging completeness and accuracy of recollection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialism (expert specialization) is essential
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The fact that success, even with the most richly-endowed natures, is only possible through specialism.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modern knowledge is highly specialized; authoritative assessment often requires specialists. Treat claims outside a witness's specialty with caution and seek testimony from domain experts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imperfections and uncertainties of memory
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Memory retains only a small fraction of impressions; recollection is fallible and reconstructive, varies with stress and time, and may omit or distort events. Evaluators should not assume memories are accurate records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceedingly narrow limitations of the senses
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The exceedingly narrow limitations of the senses.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Senses offer limited, partial access to events; sensory limitations (range, resolution, context-dependence) mean eyewitness perception can be incomplete or misleading. Independent corroboration and physiological understanding are important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best results of cerebral activity are largely involuntary/unconscious
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The fact that the best results of cerebral activity are largely involuntary, if not unconscious.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many high-quality cognitive operations (intuitions, automatic processes) are involuntary and may not be accessible to conscious report; testimony based on such processes may be difficult to articulate and requires careful interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely solely on traditional practical rules of law/logic
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Practical rules for the guidance of those who employ [testimony] are all that either logic or law has yet given… some of these practical rules are based on incorrect assumptions… they frequently lead to serious error.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal/logical traditions (e.g., blanket trust in senses, simple witness-count rules) can be inadequate; reconstruct evidentiary principles incorporating physiological and psychological science and make case-specific distinctions.
